questions.stem: Which sequence describes the normal structure of a narrative essay?
questions.explanation: A narrative sets the scene and introduces the characters (orientation), raises a problem (complication), brings it to its most intense moment (climax) and then settles it (resolution). Keeping that shape in mind prevents the commonest narrative fault, which is a story that wanders with nothing at stake.

distractorRationale.a: Reverses the sequence, so the story would end before it began
distractorRationale.c: This is the structure of an argumentative essay
distractorRationale.d: These are the features of a speech, not the stages of a story

questions.stem: Which tense is normally used to tell a story in a narrative essay?
questions.explanation: A narrative recounts events that have already happened, so the simple past is the natural base tense, with the past perfect available for anything that happened earlier still. Choosing the tense in the first sentence and holding it prevents the tense-shifting that examiners penalise.

distractorRationale.a: The present tense is used for the historic present in some literary writing, but it is hard to sustain and not expected here
distractorRationale.c: The future cannot narrate events that have already taken place
distractorRationale.d: The present perfect links past to present and cannot carry a sequence of events

questions.stem: Which sentence shows the reader the character's fear rather than simply telling it?

options.text: I was very afraid as I entered the dark corridor.
My hand stayed on the door frame long after the light had gone, and I counted my own breathing.
The corridor was dark and I felt fear in my heart.
Fear is a terrible thing, especially in a dark corridor.

questions.explanation: Showing means giving the reader the physical evidence and letting the emotion be inferred: the hand that will not let go, the counted breaths. Options a and c name the emotion outright, and option d abandons the story to comment on fear in general.

distractorRationale.a: Names the feeling and adds the weak intensifier *very*
distractorRationale.c: Also names the feeling, and *fear in my heart* is a worn phrase
distractorRationale.d: Turns the narrative into a general reflection, halting the story

questions.stem: A narrative essay may move freely between first-person *I* and third-person *he* for the same narrator.
questions.explanation: False. The narrative viewpoint must be consistent. If you begin as *I*, the whole story is told from inside that character's experience; if you begin with *he* or *she*, you stay outside. Switching confuses the reader about who is speaking and is treated as an organisation fault.

questions.stem: Which opening sentence is most likely to hold a reader's attention in a narrative essay?

options.text: In this essay I am going to narrate an experience I will never forget.
The bus had travelled only twenty minutes when the driver, without a word, pulled off the expressway and switched off the engine.
It was a beautiful morning and the birds were singing very well.
There are many experiences in life that a person can never forget.

questions.explanation: A narrative should begin inside the action, raising a question the reader wants answered: why has the driver stopped? Options a and d announce the essay instead of starting it, and option c opens with a tired scene-setting formula that promises nothing.

distractorRationale.a: Announcing your intention wastes the opening and delays the story
distractorRationale.c: A cliché opening that creates no tension and no specific detail
distractorRationale.d: A general statement about life rather than the beginning of a story

questions.stem: Which line of dialogue is punctuated correctly?

options.text: "Move to the back of the bus" the conductor shouted.
"Move to the back of the bus," the conductor shouted.
"Move to the back of the bus," The conductor shouted.
Move to the back of the bus, "the conductor shouted".

questions.explanation: The spoken words are enclosed in quotation marks and separated from the reporting phrase by a comma placed inside the closing mark. The reporting phrase is part of the same sentence, so *the* stays in lower case and the full stop closes everything at the end.

distractorRationale.a: Omits the comma before the closing quotation mark
distractorRationale.c: Capitalises *The* as though the reporting phrase were a new sentence
distractorRationale.d: Puts the quotation marks round the reporting phrase instead of the speech

questions.stem: Why is the ending "...and then I woke up and realised it was all a dream" a weak resolution?

options.text: It cancels the events of the story, so the complication is never really resolved
Dreams may not be mentioned in a narrative essay
It uses the wrong tense for a narrative

questions.explanation: A resolution should settle the problem the story raised. Declaring the whole thing a dream withdraws everything that has happened, so the reader is left with no outcome at all. Examiners see this ending constantly and treat it as a failure of planning.

distractorRationale.a: The sentence is perfectly grammatical; the fault is structural
distractorRationale.c: A dream may certainly feature in a story — the problem is using it to erase the plot
distractorRationale.d: The tense is the correct simple past

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the past perfect to signal a flashback within a past-tense narrative?

options.text: I sat on the bench and remember that my father warns me about that road.
I sat on the bench and remembered that my father had warned me about that road.
I sit on the bench and remembered that my father warned me about that road.
I sat on the bench and remembered that my father will warn me about that road.

questions.explanation: The narrative runs in the simple past — *sat*, *remembered* — and the warning happened before that moment, so it takes the past perfect *had warned*. This is how a writer steps back in time without confusing the reader about the order of events.

distractorRationale.a: Shifts into the present with *remember* and *warns*, breaking the narrative tense
distractorRationale.c: Opens in the present *sit* and then jumps to the past, an unmotivated shift
distractorRationale.d: *Will warn* places the warning in the future, contradicting the memory

questions.stem: A candidate's narrative contains this sentence: "The market was very very noisy and there were plenty of people making a lot of noise everywhere." What is the main weakness?

options.text: It is repetitive and vague, offering no specific sensory detail

questions.explanation: The sentence says the same thing three times — noisy, plenty of people, a lot of noise — without letting the reader hear anything. A stronger version names particular sounds: "Three radios competed from three stalls, and a woman was calling the price of dried fish over all of them."

distractorRationale.b: The tense is correctly the simple past
distractorRationale.c: The clauses are joined by *and*, so there is no comma splice
distractorRationale.d: The point of view is consistent throughout the sentence

questions.stem: In a narrative essay of about 450 words, roughly how much space should the orientation occupy?

options.text: About half the essay, so that the setting is fully described
One short paragraph, just enough to establish place, time and the main character
No space at all; the story should begin at the climax
Three paragraphs, one for the place, one for the time and one for each character

questions.explanation: The reader needs only enough grounding to follow the action, so one economical paragraph is right. Long scene-setting delays the complication, and since the marks reward a shaped story rather than a description, the bulk of the essay should be spent on what happens.

distractorRationale.a: Half the essay spent on setting leaves too little room for the plot
distractorRationale.c: Some grounding is needed or the reader cannot follow the events
distractorRationale.d: Separate paragraphs for each element make the opening mechanical and slow

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the complication in a narrative essay?
questions.explanation: The complication is crucial as it introduces the main conflict or tension that drives the narrative forward. Without a complication, the story may lack engagement and depth, making it less interesting for the reader.

distractorRationale.a: While introducing the main character is important, it is not the purpose of the complication.
distractorRationale.c: Summarizing the story is not part of the complication; it typically occurs in the conclusion.
distractorRationale.d: The resolution comes after the complication, serving to resolve the conflict.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the use of sensory details in a narrative essay?

options.text: They are used to describe the plot.
They help the reader to visualize and experience the story.
They are irrelevant to the narrative.

questions.explanation: Sensory details engage the reader's senses, allowing them to visualize the setting, feel the emotions, and experience the story more vividly. This enhances the storytelling by creating a more immersive experience.

distractorRationale.a: Sensory details do not describe the plot; they enhance the experience of it.
distractorRationale.c: Summarizing main events is not the function of sensory details.
distractorRationale.d: Sensory details are crucial for creating an engaging narrative.

questions.stem: In a narrative essay, what is meant by maintaining a consistent narrative viewpoint?

options.text: Using various points of view throughout the essay.
Sticking to one perspective throughout the story.

questions.explanation: Maintaining a consistent narrative viewpoint means that the essay should stick to one perspective, whether first-person or third-person, to avoid confusing the reader. This consistency helps the reader connect with the story more effectively.

distractorRationale.a: Using various points of view can confuse the reader and disrupt the flow of the narrative.
distractorRationale.c: Changing tense frequently can also confuse the narrative structure.
distractorRationale.d: While including multiple characters' thoughts can be engaging, it must be done within a consistent viewpoint.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences contains a strong sensory detail?

questions.explanation: The sentence describing the cake's smell uses sensory details that evoke taste and smell, making it more vivid and engaging for the reader. Strong sensory details help the reader to visualize and experience the moment.

distractorRationale.a: This sentence is vague and does not engage the reader's senses.
distractorRationale.c: While it conveys enjoyment, it lacks sensory detail.
distractorRationale.d: The timing of when the cake was baked does not provide any sensory experience.

questions.stem: What role does dialogue play in a narrative essay?

options.text: It serves to summarize the plot.
It reveals character and advances the story.
It is used to create confusion.
It is irrelevant to the narrative.

questions.explanation: Dialogue is essential in narrative essays as it reveals character traits and motivations, while also advancing the plot. Well-placed dialogue can make the characters feel more real and relatable to the reader.

distractorRationale.a: Dialogue does not summarize the plot; it adds depth to the characters and events.
distractorRationale.c: Good dialogue should enhance clarity, not create confusion.
distractorRationale.d: Dialogue is a key element in narrative writing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a strong resolution in a narrative essay?

options.text: And then everything went back to normal.
After much struggle, she finally found her way home.
And then they lived happily ever after.

questions.explanation: A strong resolution provides closure and reflects on the journey of the characters. The option that describes the character's struggle and resolution offers a more satisfying conclusion to the narrative.

distractorRationale.a: This resolution is vague and does not provide closure.
distractorRationale.c: Simply stating 'The end' lacks depth and does not resolve the narrative.
distractorRationale.d: While classic, 'happily ever after' can be overly simplistic and unoriginal.

distractorRationale.a: Orientation is a key component that sets the stage for the story.
distractorRationale.b: Complication is essential for creating conflict in the narrative.
distractorRationale.c: Resolution is necessary to conclude the narrative effectively.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences maintains a consistent past tense throughout?

options.text: He walked to the store and buys some milk.
She was running when she sees the dog.

questions.explanation: The sentence 'They played soccer and then went home' maintains a consistent past tense, which is essential for narrative clarity. Consistency in tense helps the reader follow the story without confusion.

distractorRationale.a: This sentence shifts from past to present tense, disrupting the narrative flow.
distractorRationale.b: This sentence also shifts tense, which can confuse the reader.

questions.stem: How can a writer effectively create tension in a narrative essay?

distractorRationale.a: Too much background information can slow down the narrative and reduce tension.
distractorRationale.c: Quick summaries can diminish the suspense and excitement of the story.
distractorRationale.d: Relying solely on dialogue may not provide enough context or tension.

questions.stem: What is the effect of using dialogue in a narrative essay?

distractorRationale.a: While dialogue can affect pacing, its primary function is to enhance character development.
distractorRationale.c: Dialogue complements sensory details rather than replacing them.
